FeatFloWer · design document · drafted 2026-07-31

DNS (FBM) validation campaignStages D0 – D6, from recertification to the Endgegner cases

Companion to the completed EL campaign (docs/md_docs/el_validation_report.md); reuses its discipline, tooling and report/datasheet/RUNBOOK format.

Target end state: the resolved-particle DNS method (Fictitious Boundary Method + PE rigid-body backend) is understood, documented and validated to the same depth as the EL method — so both can be used selectively, and DNS can serve as in-house ground truth for EL closures (“DNS-informed EL”).

The deeper motivation (R. Münster, 2026-08-01): pre-campaign DNS studies with this codebase — the Kroupa-box effective-viscosity study and the Archimedes-tube-crystallizer slug — did produce correct physics, but only through painful trial-and-error on resolution, dt, collision handling and meshing. The campaign's yardstick is that such cases become set-up-able in an informed, structured way from written guidelines (D1–D3), first-time-right at predictable cost. That claim is tested literally: both pain-cases return as the D6 capstone (“Endgegner”) stage.

§0

What we are validating — method map

From code survey 2026-07-31

The DNS method in FeatFloWer is the Turek/Wan FBM:

Representation
Per-Q2-DOF 0/1 indicator FictKNPR, rebuilt from scratch every step by geometric point-in-body queries (source/src_quadLS/QuadSc_boundary.f90:60 → fbm_updateFBMGeom, source/src_fbm/fbm_main.f90). PE backend classifier supports spheres, capsules, boxes, ellipsoids, cylinders, triangle meshes (libs/pe/src/interface/object_queries.cpp). Optional HashGrid acceleration (SimPar@UseHashGridAccel).
No-slip
Internal Dirichlet by row filtering — solution values set to the rigid-body field v = V + ω×(x−x_c), defect zeroed, matrix rows unit-diagonalized (Boundary_QuadScalar_Val/Def/Mat, QuadSc_boundary.f90:542-728). No penalty, no forcing term.
Hydrodynamic force / torque
Volume integral of (−pI + μ(∇u+∇uᵀ))·(−∇α) over the interface band (ForcesLocalParticles, source/src_quadLS/QuadSc_force_extension.f90:24; KVEL-accelerated serial variant in QuadSc_force_serial.f90).
Rigid-body update & collisions
PE HardContactEulerLagrange (PGS, velocity-level contacts) with optional Kroupa lubrication; serial-PE mode (per-rank full-domain PE world, forces summed over the CFD comm) or parallel-PE mode (rank 0 excluded, Cartesian decomposition, shadow copies). FullC0ntact is a second backend (not in scope for this campaign except where an app forces it).
Time stepping
Fixed dt from SimPar@TimeStep. TimeStepCtrl exists but every DNS call site is commented out; bGapAdaptiveTimeStep is a declared, unused stub. ComputeCFL prints fluid + particle CFL but nothing acts on it.
Mesh
Fixed uniform multigrid hierarchy (1:8 refinement, SimPar@MinMeshLevel/MaxMeshLevel). No dynamic refinement around particles; r-adaptivity machinery (UmbrellaSmoother with distance-to-body monitor) exists but is not wired into the DNS loop.

The “L3 within ~2% of PIV” claim has no in-repo evidence (missing tc-ref/ PIV CSVs, missing guide_02_part2).

§1

Campaign principles — inherited from the EL campaign, binding

  1. Probe-first: one short smoke gated before any sweep. Every case has a RUNBOOK.md (design → gates → job numbers → verdicts); every quantitative claim becomes a datasheet row (expected / source / measured / tolerance / verdict). FAILs recorded honestly with attribution, never tuned around.

  2. Independent estimators beat tighter tolerances (the EL Couette lesson): wherever possible each stage carries two routes to the same number (e.g. force-integral vs momentum-balance; wall force vs bed weight).

  3. Bitwise twins + A/B worktrees settle “pre-existing vs ours”.

  4. Master/worker asymmetry discipline: rank 0 has no PE in parallel mode; diagnostics must be collective-safe in rank-asymmetric paths.

  5. Mesh fixtures need git add -f (.gitignore excludes *.tri/*.par); per-case pinned example.json (never the shared libs/pe/pe/interface/example.json scratch file).

  6. The user pushes; agent commits only. FF commits end with the standard Co-Authored-By line. Never push libs/pe.

Campaign artifacts mirror the EL set

  • docs/md_docs/dns_validation_report.md — the science record.
  • docs/md_docs/dns_validation_datasheet.md + .csv — same columns as EL (suite | case | quantity | expected | expected_source | measured | rel_error | tolerance | verdict).
  • Per-case RUNBOOKs under applications/<app>/validation_cases/<case>/.
  • docs/md_docs/dns_practitioners_guide.md — the usability deliverable: resolution guidelines, dt guidelines, mode selection (serial vs parallel PE), lubrication-threshold rules, staging/submission recipes. This is a first-class output of Stages 1–2, not an afterthought.
  • Dashboard extension (docs/dashboard/) once the datasheet exists.

Every FAIL is attributed to a documented cause rather than left open — the E1 low-Re deficit, for instance, is a sim-vs-experiment gap present in the 2002 paper itself. Every verdict count above is a settled reading. Two closures landed on 2026-08-22. The D3.2 wide-column discriminator fleet — 7 jobs, 140208–140214 — is complete and settles the attribution: the confined exponent is a confinement law carried by collective return flow, not per-particle wall drag. And a solver defect found in the certified binary lineage (hcaf_angvel_reset, angular velocity zeroed every step) retires the D2.3 “frictional stall” as an artifact — on the repaired binary the frictional DKT run tumbles. The blind-bore cell that produced the first Einstein-gate attempt was retired on 2026-08-26 — 45.7% of its torque was generated in particle-free fluid, so η(φ) = T(φ)/T(0) came out dilution-contaminated; that FAIL verdict is revised to RECORDED in the datasheet and its resolution reading withdrawn, which is why the FAIL count reads 2. The replacement, a through-hole annulus with symmetry ends, passes all four baseline gates against an exact analytic torque (the corrected reaction estimator lands on T_exact to five digits) and has now measured three concentrations. V1’s apparent failure was the instrument, not the physics. The first production use of the D2.2 sub-grid lubrication add-on rides along as controlled twins and is now settled: lubrication adds +2.7% at φ = 0.20 and +0.8% at φ = 0.10. The apparent non-decay on the first segments was a window artifact — flagged as such when it was recorded — and the extensions show the contribution decaying 3.6×, tracking the near-contact pair count. In parallel, finalising the drag benchmarks for the CHERD journal supplement continues — that is where four of the RESOLVED rows came from: two errata, a metrology discovery, and a 24-run re-measurement campaign that left every headline number intact.

Benchmark 1 — ten Cate sphere sedimentation (E1–E4)

Setup & expectation

A single d = 15 mm sphere settles under gravity in a closed 100 × 100 × 160 mm box of silicone oil, filmed by particle-image velocimetry (ten Cate et al., 2002). Four variants change the oil viscosity to sweep Re from 1.5 to 31.9, so one geometry exercises the Stokes, intermediate and inertial regimes in turn. The gate is the peak settling velocity against the paper's printed Table II ratios, with the trajectory shape checked against the PIV curve.

Reference audit — the gate reference changed

ten Cate Table II (p. 4018) supersedes the digitized curves for peak gates

The paper prints experimental u_max/u_∞ = 0.947 / 0.953 / 0.959 / 0.955 for E1–E4. Measured against those printed values, the digitized E1 and E2 curve peaks are +3.4% and +3.9% too fast; E3 and E4 are clean (within 0.7%). Peak gates therefore now use the Table II printed values; the digitized curves are kept for shape comparison only.

Cross-case finding — the spatial error is geometry-dominated

The E2–E4 ladders are nearly identical (within ~0.5 pp at every level) despite an 8× range in Re, and the L3→L4 shift is uniform (−2.1…−2.4 pp) across all four cases. The spatial error at these resolutions is therefore set by the interface representation of the sphere, not by the flow regime. E1's overall offset is its sim-vs-experiment reference gap, not different discretization behavior.

Timestep — the dt window is accuracy-bounded only

No stability floor: choose dt by error budget

The coupling stays stable all the way down the ladder — E4 L3 at dt = 0.25 ms runs clean, with 0 sawtooth warnings and a peak of +1.94%, and the DKT density-ratio probes are clean at dt = 0.5–1.0 ms. Smaller dt buys nothing in stability and moves peaks toward the positive spatial error, so dt is chosen against the accuracy budget, not against a stability limit.

Config rule (fatal-guarded): the deck's SimPar@TimeStep and the case json's stepsize_ must be equal — PE takes its step from the json. A mismatch aborts at step 1 with a diagnostic.

Shipped hardening — runs report their own trouble

DNS_SAWTOOTH_WARNING runtime watchdog

An amplitude-gated alternation detector in var_QuadScalar, emitted identically in both PE modes: it catches a particle velocity trace that starts flipping sign step to step — the signature of a coupling that has gone bad — and says so in the log instead of letting the run finish quietly. Validated by two controls: on a deliberately unstable trajectory it fires at t = 0.0293 s, while the velocity excursion is still small (before |v_z| crosses 0.2 m/s), and on a healthy run it produces zero warnings over 300 steps including peak acceleration.

Headline finding — E1 converges onto ten Cate's own LBM, not onto the experiment

The ~5% low-Re gap is sim-vs-experiment, and it is in the 2002 paper too

E1 at L4 gave −5.23% vs experiment: refinement moves away from the measurement on clean trajectories, so the deficit is not an interface-resolution artifact. Sim-vs-sim tells the other half of the story — our finest configs match ten Cate's own Table II S-series LBM ratios at all four Re. Their base LBM S1 is itself −5.6% vs experiment. At Re ≲ 2 the reference band must include the paper's own simulation values, not just the experiment.

Benchmark 2 — Hasimoto periodic array drag (D1.1) CLOSED

Hasimoto's 1959 paper is applied mathematics, not a simulation study, and the problem it settles is a specific one. Build the Stokes flow through a periodic array of spheres the obvious way — by superposing the disturbance each sphere would produce in isolation — and the lattice sum diverges. Burgers had pointed this out in 1941, and the models that followed (his own diffuse force field, Brinkman, Debye & Bueche) worked around the divergence rather than resolving it.

Hasimoto's resolution is to expand velocity and pressure as Fourier series over the reciprocal lattice and then take seriously what the k = 0 mode says. It gives P₀ = F/τ₀ (eq. 2.14): the force on each sphere is balanced by a mean pressure gradient across the unit cell of volume τ₀. That term is not optional bookkeeping — omitting it is precisely what makes the sums diverge, and with it in place they are finite. The remaining sums are then evaluated by Ewald's theta-transformation, the same device used to compute Madelung constants for ionic crystals; in Hasimoto's reading the lattice behaves like unit charges embedded in a neutralizing uniform background, and that background is the mean pressure gradient.

Applied to a dilute cubic lattice of spheres of radius a, the result gives the drag on any one sphere as a function of volume concentration alone: F = 6πμaU / (1 − κa), with κa = 1.7601 φ1/3 for the simple-cubic lattice (his Table 1), and the §5 refinement carrying it to K = 1/(1 − 1.7601 φ1/3 + φ − 1.5593 φ²). K exceeds 1 always: each sphere sits in flow already retarded by its own periodic images, so an array drags harder than an isolated sphere.

For validating the FBM that combination is unusually good. The reference is analytic — no measurement uncertainty in the target, unlike a PIV curve. The flow is genuinely periodic, so it exercises exactly the machinery a walled case like ten Cate can never touch (as this campaign found out the hard way). And the Stokes regime removes inertia, time accuracy and particle motion from the comparison, leaving the spatial discretization of the interface as essentially the only error source left standing.

Setup & expectation

A single fixed sphere of radius r = 1/6 sits at the centre of a periodic unit cell, which makes it one member of an infinite simple-cubic array at solid fraction φ = 0.0194. A uniform body force drives Stokes flow through the cell (Re ≈ 3 × 10⁻³) and the measured drag is compared with Hasimoto's 1959 dilute-array expansion, which gives K = 1.8322 at this φ. Nothing moves, so the case isolates the accuracy of the fictitious-boundary force integral on a stationary interface. It also turned out to be the only case in either campaign that genuinely exercises periodic boundaries — which is how it found the defect below.

The campaign's headline: a ladder that converged beautifully — onto the wrong answer

The first four rungs converged at apparent order ~1.7 — and settled on a −8.9% asymptote. A convergent ladder that misses the analytic value cannot be a resolution problem, and the walled ten Cate case already certified the same force integral to +0.03% against ten Cate's LBM. That pointed at the one ingredient the walled case never touches: periodicity.

A code trace found it. The Q2/E013 communicator was built by a non-periodic octree search, so it contained zero periodic DOF pairs — and that communicator gates every Q2 exchange and the parallel pressure solve. Every “periodic” face in the code base was in fact being solved traction-free. A decisive experiment confirmed it before any code was written: on a plane that periodicity makes a symmetry plane, max|u_x| / max|u_z| came out at 0.102 — the faces were breathing at 10% of the driving velocity.

The fix (2026-08-03) and the gates it had to pass

parentcomm.f90 now builds a second, parallel periodic vertex-share table (myVERTLINKPER) and unions it into the Q2 communicator gate. The probe has to sweep all 26 periodic images: single-axis probing leaves edge and corner DOFs partially coupled on a 3×3×3 torus and diverged to NaN — periodic edges and corners matter as much as faces.

  • PASSWalled bitwise twin — a non-periodic deck reruns byte-identical on the new binary. The fix is a strict no-op off the periodic path, so every walled ten Cate result stands untouched.
  • PASSu_x plane test — the symmetry-plane ratio drops from 0.102 to 1.75 × 10⁻⁹, and matched points on opposite faces agree to 1 × 10⁻²⁰. The faces are genuinely coupled.
  • PASSCommunicator census — PERIODIC_COMM reports 702 = 27 × 26 neighbour pairs on the QBOX9 torus (every rank now neighbours every other rank), 386 of them periodic-only and previously absent entirely.
  • PASSEL momentum re-check — the EL campaign's Newton-pair gate, rerun on the fixed binary: residual 5.08 × 10⁻²¹, drift 5.32 × 10⁻⁸. Both hold, now on a box that is actually periodic.
  • guardsTwo failure modes are now refused rather than mis-solved: MUMPS as coarse solver on periodic decks (the global numbering swaps periodic labels instead of merging them), and non-axis-uniform partitions — periodic runs need a Cartesian axis-uniform partition so subdomain faces coincide with their images, and METIS graph partitions are invalid.

Conventions pinned from the source paper — the raw table above is Hasimoto's convention

Both halves of “which force against which velocity” were read off literature/hasimoto_1959.pdf rather than assumed. Eq. (2.14), P₀ = F/τ₀: the sphere force balances the mean pressure gradient over the whole cell, so under body-force driving F = f · V_cell — exactly the force the diagnostic measures. Eqs. (2.5) and (4.7–4.8): the U in F = 6πμaU·K is v₀, the k = 0 Fourier mode, i.e. the whole-cell volume average — the superficial (Darcy) velocity. The interstitial-velocity variant leaves −2.2%, which is the O(φ) convention gap and not a discretization defect.

Closure — the residual ladder is fully itemized, nothing unexplained

Two measurable discretization terms account for what is left. First, the indicator-volume error per rung, taken from each run's own fluid fraction against the analytic 0.9806075: the L2 discrete sphere is +0.95% in radius, L3 is −0.43%, L4/L5 are ≲0.05%. Second, once each rung is corrected for its own volume error, the ladder becomes near-first-order (orders 0.76 → 1.18) with a level-constant interface coefficient — a_eff ≈ a − 0.14 h. That constancy across levels is the falsifiable content; the uncorrected version drifts and the model fails.

Richardson extrapolation of the corrected ladder gives K∞ = 1.821…1.825, i.e. −0.4…−0.6% against the analytic 1.8322 — closing within resolution uncertainty. The full error budget reads: traction-free faces (fixed) + indicator-volume error (measured per rung) + an O(h) interface term (the remainder).

Erratum (2026-08-15) — the sign of the interface model was wrong RESOLVED

Preparing the CHERD supplement forced the near-interface model to be re-derived with explicit sign tracking, and it came out backwards. The model had been recorded as a_eff = a + 0.14 h — “no-slip felt out into the fluid”. But the sensitivity is d ln K / d ln a = 1 + 3φ · d ln K_ref/dφ = +1.77 at the ladder's φ, i.e. positive: an enlarged effective radius would raise the measured K. Every ladder rung and every probe sits below the reference. The deficits therefore require the opposite sign — a_eff = a − 0.14 h.

The physical reading flips with it, and is the more plausible one: the flow effectively penetrates ~0.14 h into the nominal solid, because the discrete constraint under-enforces no-slip between velocity nodes. Re-derived per level from deficit ÷ sensitivity, the implied coefficient reads c = 0.10 / 0.17 / 0.16 / 0.18 at L2–L5, and the post-fix calibration figures r_h/r = 1.034 / 1.028 / 1.013 correspond to a_eff/a = 0.966 / 0.972 / 0.987.

Every quantitative result stands. The campaign's arithmetic always used the deficit form — the coarse-probe blind predictions (−12.1% / −10.0% at D/h = 3/4), the Richardson closure, the array-level correction factor. Only the narrative sign flips. This page is one of the affected records and is corrected here; the D1.1 RUNBOOK and the practitioner's guide are corrected alongside it.

  • PASSMomentum balance closes at every rung — the independent estimator (steady drag vs applied forcing f·V) agrees to 0.05–0.15%, before and after the fix. It was blind to the defect, which is precisely why the second estimator mattered.
  • calibrationr_h/r re-measured post-fix: 1.034 / 1.028 / 1.013 at D/h = 6/12/24 — roughly half the pre-fix figures and now clearly shrinking with h. Most of what had looked like an FBM effective-radius offset was the traction-free box. The remainder is still the ten Cate section IV-C phenomenon (their LBM needed r_h/r₀ = 1.12 at D/h ≈ 8), at much smaller magnitude.
  • RESOLVEDThe φ = 0.0082 anomaly — for a long time the campaign's most stubborn open question — is closed by the recheck below.
Independent cross-check at a second volume fraction — the closure model holds, and the last open thread closes

The closure above was built on a single φ, so the honest test is a different one. The φ = 0.0082 case (r = 0.125, D/h = 18) is the natural candidate, and it had been the campaign's most stubborn anomaly: a deficit roughly twice the main ladder's at matched resolution, which defeated the radius, confinement and parasitic-drag explanations one after another. Rerun on the fixed binary it gives K = 1.5071 against the analytic 1.5304 — −1.52%, where before the fix it read −19.2%.

So the anomaly was the traction-free box all along, and it punished the more dilute case harder. That matches the image-strength reading taken at the time, which found only ~45% of the confinement captured at φ = 0.0082 against ~80% at φ = 0.019 — a smaller sphere leans more heavily on its periodic images, so losing them costs more. What remains is ordinary O(h) interface widening: the implied coefficient is c ≈ 0.09 at D/h = 18 (using the φ-correct sensitivity 1.506) against the main ladder's 0.12–0.17, and the indicator-volume error here is negligible at ΔV/V = +7 × 10⁻⁴. The same two-term error model, at a φ it was not fitted to.

One caveat, kept rather than tidied away: the settled force overshoots f·V_cell by +0.96% — essentially unchanged from the pre-fix +0.97%, so it is not a periodicity artifact. It was read at the time as something case-specific — the off-centre sphere at 0.375³, plus a slow settling tail — and that attribution has since been superseded by the functional-closure measurement below. Reading K with the momentum-balance force instead gives −2.46%. Both readings close the anomaly; neither is hidden.

New metrology finding — the force functional overshoots by a uniform ~2% RECORDED

Assembling the CHERD supplement meant checking one thing that had never been checked across cases: the summed per-particle α-gradient force functional against the fluid-phase momentum balance, which at steady state must be (1 − φ)·f·V. It is not. The functional measures 1.02 × (1 − φ) f V — +1.9…+2.0% at L4 across every array point (φ = 0.05/0.10/0.20/0.30, Re 0–30), +2.03…+2.10% along the whole d11 ladder L2–L5, and +1.8…+2.8% once the coarse probes and the φ = 0.0082 case are included. It is level-independent and φ-independent: a small uniform overshoot of the force-evaluation integral itself, not a resolution effect.

That single number supersedes the “off-centre-sphere effect” attribution given to the earlier F-vs-f·V overshoots — the φ = 0.0082 case's +0.96% and the coarse probes' +1.7% and +2.6% are all consistent with the uniform +2% once referenced to (1 − φ) f V rather than to f V. The reason the main d11 ladder appeared to close f·V to 0.1% is a coincidence of its own packing fraction: at φ = 0.0194, 1.02 × (1 − φ) = 1.0002. A benchmark that agrees to a suspiciously round accuracy at exactly one φ was hiding a systematic, and it took the whole matrix to see it.

Mechanism OPEN — quadrature of ∇α over the interface band is the leading suspect, but nothing is claimed. Recorded, not attributed.

supersededAn earlier reading of this benchmark quoted an “exterior convention” ladder (−13.1 / −12.2 / −9.9 / −9.2%, r_h/r 1.078…1.053) built on f·V_fluid. It is superseded twice over — the numbers were pre-fix, and eq. (2.14) settles the convention the other way.

Applied to production resolution — what D/h = 3–4 actually buys RECORDED

The ladder above starts at D/h = 6 and climbs to 48. Real production work — the studies that motivated this campaign — ran at D/h = 3–4, below the bottom rung, and the practitioner's question is simply how wrong that is. Two ~3-minute probes answer it directly: keep the L2 mesh and shrink the sphere instead of refining, giving r = 1/12 (D/h = 3) and r = 1/9 (D/h = 4), each judged against Hasimoto's K at its own φ. Because this is a closed benchmark being applied rather than a new one, it is a probe, not a rung.

Both land in the same place: the drag is about 10% low, and the closure model built on the fine ladder still describes it. The a_eff = a − 0.14 h model was used to predict both deficits blind — −12.1% and −10.0% — and landed within 1–3 pp of what the probes measured, with an implied coefficient c = (a − a_eff)/h of 0.10–0.15 against the fine ladder's 0.12–0.17. That extends the model's verified range down to D/h = 3, which is where it is actually needed.

Both are quoted rather than one being chosen.

Practitioner verdict — reading a production run at D/h = 3–4
  • correctableMean drag comes out at ≈ 90% of true — low by 9–12%, but systematically low, not randomly. It is therefore correctable: the solver behaves as if each sphere were 0.14 h smaller than nominal, so boost drags by sens(φ)·0.14·h/a to recover the nominal radius. A known bias with a model is a far better position than an unknown one.
  • noiseIndividual particle forces carry roughly 8–15% rms grid noise at these resolutions, extrapolating the O(h) noise floor down from the measured ladder. Collective quantities — mean drag, bed pressure drop, effective viscosity — average this away; a single particle's trajectory does not.
  • sub-gridEverything within ~2 cells of contact is sub-grid (the D2.1 crossover rule), and at D/h = 3–4 two cells is half a diameter. All near-contact physics is therefore the contact model's job, not the flow solver's — which makes contact parameters physics to be tuned, exactly as the DKT friction finding concluded.
  • confirmedThe same question asked of a crowd rather than one sphere gives the same answer: the production-resolution array runs in D3.1 land at 84–87% of converged mean drag with a single 1.15–1.20 correction. Single-sphere and array-level evidence agree.

caveatThe probes shrank the sphere at fixed mesh, so φ fell along with D/h and the two are conflated. At a production-scale φ the sensitivity factor is larger and the D/h = 3 deficit is a few points worse than measured here. What transfers is the c coefficient, not the literal percentage.

Benchmark 3 — drafting–kissing–tumbling (D2.3) CLOSED

Setup & expectation

Two equal spheres are released in-line, one above the other, in a closed 6d × 6d × 24d column at Galileo number Ga ≈ 80. The classical expectation (Fortes, Joseph & Lundgren 1987; Glowinski et al. 2001) is a three-phase sequence: the trailing sphere is drafted into the leader's wake and accelerates, the pair kisses and falls briefly as a doublet, then the doublet is unstable broadside-on and tumbles apart. Because the sequence is symmetry-breaking and chaotic after contact, the gates are mechanism-level — phase sequence and kissing time, not point values.

Axisymmetric smoke — drafting and kissing confirmed

Drafting is unambiguous over t ≈ 10–18: the trailing sphere reaches −0.499 against the leader's −0.427. Kissing follows with the gap locking at 1.000 d at t_kiss ≈ 18.1, after which the doublet falls at a common, still-accelerating velocity. Tumbling is absent, exactly as expected from a perfectly axisymmetric initial condition (lateral drift 4 × 10⁻⁴). 0 sawtooth warnings. PASS

Offset variant — the tilt starts, then stalls dead in contact

Seeding the asymmetry (trailer displaced x = +0.05 d) reproduces drafting and kissing at t_kiss ≈ 18.04, and the tilt then grows during kissing to ≈ 4.2° — the tumbling mechanism starting up exactly as Fortes describes. Then it stops, by t = 25, with the pair in exact contact. Three candidates were on the table: an under-resolved wake at D/h = 8, contact-friction locking, or simply not enough run time. RECORDED

Elimination 1 — double the wake resolution: the stall does not move

The D/h = 16 rung (job 137733, 109 ranks, 30 h) reproduces drafting and kissing cleanly — t_kiss = 18.34 against 18.04 at D/h = 8, so the kissing timing is near resolution-independent (+1.7%) — and then locks at 4.0°, in exact contact (separation 1.0000), against 4.2° on the coarse mesh. The stall is resolution-independent, so the wake-resolution hypothesis is refuted. The same run also disposes of the patience hypothesis: the residual tilt drift is 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ per time unit, which would need roughly 3000 time units to tumble. The doublet just falls rigidly at a common velocity (v_z = −0.55 at t = 25). RECORDED

Elimination 2 — switch off contact friction: the tumble unlocks immediately

Same D/h = 8 case, same everything, with staticFriction_ = dynamicFriction_ = 0 (job 137877). After t_kiss = 18.04 the tilt grows 4.8° → 22.3° over t = 19…25, at an accelerating rate, with the pair visibly rolling around its contact point and still mid-tumble when the run ends. With friction on it locks near 4° at both resolutions; with friction off it tumbles. That is a clean one-variable experiment. PASS

The extension runs it out — the complete Fortes sequence, ending in a role exchange

Carried to t = 40 (job 137965), the frictionless case produces the textbook sequence end to end: kiss at t = 18.04, then rolling contact with the tilt passing 22.3° at t = 25 and 43.3° at t = 28; separation begins at t = 29.64 while the pair is still rotating; the pair lies horizontal at t = 32.92; and by t = 40 the spheres are 2.37 d apart at 109°.

The ending is the detail that makes it convincing: the two have exchanged roles. The former trailer is now the lower sphere and falling faster (−0.419 against −0.348) — the drafting partner overtakes and becomes the leader, which is precisely what Fortes, Joseph & Lundgren describe. D2.3 is closed. PASS

Erratum (2026-08-22) — the “frictional stall” was a solver defect, not a contact model RESOLVED

Porting the D2.2 lubrication add-on needed a rotation-preserving test host, and reading the owner code for it surfaced a line that had been sitting in the certified binary lineage the whole time: HardContactAndFluid::integratePositions contained an unconditional w = Vec3(0,0,0) — an atc-era debug artifact that zeroed every particle's angular velocity at every step. Every campaign particle was integrated as a non-rotating rigid body. The certified DKT log shows it in the act: angular velocity is exactly 0.0 at all 10 000 records while the hydrodynamic torque is nonzero (max |τ| = 1.02 × 10⁻²) — torque computed, fed in, and discarded.

That makes rolling kinematically impossible, and rolling is how a doublet tumbles about its contact. So any tangential friction froze the tilt, at any resolution — which is exactly the “resolution-independent model property” the elimination above measured. The apparent resolution-independence belonged to the defect, not to the physics.

Fixed upstream (libs/pe ≥ de855b6, campaign pin now f9b7115), and every submodule bump was twin-gated before it was believed: G0a reproduced the certified e4_l3 settling log byte-for-byte on every stream — across CPU generations, which is a stronger match than same-node — because at ω ≈ 0 the fix must be inert; G0b then re-ran the DKT twin as a report-only physics diff and found textbook causal ordering: the ω columns and the torque diverge first, at step 3, and position and velocity follow one step later. Rotation is real feedback, not roundoff — the trailer's y-torque drops ≈ 40% once it is allowed to spin with the local shear. The FBM does impose ω × r into the fluid Dirichlet values, so restored rotation couples hydrodynamically at first order.

The discriminator (job 140410, deck byte-identical to certified, full 5000 steps): the drafting phase is untouched — t_kiss = 18.095 against 18.100 — and then the two runs separate qualitatively. Certified: 3.89° at kiss creeping to 4.21° at t = 25, fitted growth 0.002/t.u., doubling time 364 t.u. — a genuine stall. Repaired: 3.54° at kiss growing exponentially to 16.17°, rate 0.232/t.u., doubling every 3.0 t.u. and still accelerating at the end of the window. End state: the certified pair falls as a locked rigid body (both spheres exactly −0.5620), the repaired pair splits (leader −0.5445, trailer −0.5621) as the trailer swings past.

What it means, and the rule that follows

Friction does not pin the contact. With ω ≡ 0, rolling was impossible and any tangential traction froze the tilt; on a consistent binary friction modulates the tumble instead of suppressing it — 16.17° under the HCAF default μ_s/μ_d = 0.1/0.05 against 21.70° frictionless, at the same t = 25, a retardation of ≈ 25% in tilt at matched time. That pair is now a single-binary controlled comparison (both curves at pe f9b7115, decks differing only in the two friction coefficients, drafting byte-identical across all 720 shared pre-contact samples and t_kiss = 18.095 for both); the earlier 22.29° comparator was measured on the ω-zeroed binary, and the fix moves the frictionless trajectory by only ≈ 2.7% — second-order, as predicted. The full 90° passage lies beyond this window (extrapolating to t ≈ 30–32). The earlier reading — “a dry frictional contact freezes the Fortes instability” — is retired.

What survives is the physical argument, now a quantitative modeling choice rather than the difference between tumbling and not tumbling: two real spheres touching in a liquid ride a lubrication film that transmits essentially no tangential traction, so a dry frictional contact overstates tangential coupling. Guideline for DKT-class simulations: prefer ~zero contact friction, or a lubricated-contact model. The transferable lesson stands in a sharper form — contact parameters are physics, not stabilizers, and so is anything in the integrator that silently discards a degree of freedom. Neither fired a diagnostic.

Detection note, for anyone on an older binary: if libs/pe predates de855b6, all rotation-coupled results are suspect — check for w = Vec3(0,0,0) in HardContactAndFluid::integratePositions, or simply verify that DNS_PART_STATE angular velocities are not exactly zero for all time under nonzero torque. Impact triage: settling, drag and array results (ten Cate, D3.1, D3.2) are unaffected — those flows are near-axisymmetric with spin ≈ 0, so the fix is inert there, and G0a proves it bitwise. DKT was the one case where it was first order.

supersededThe pre-2026-08-22 reading of this benchmark — “contact-friction locking pins the contact and suppresses the Fortes instability, resolution-independently” — is superseded by the erratum above. The frictionless results (tumble, separation, role exchange) are unaffected: at zero friction the tangential channel is off either way. Practitioner's guide §6 carries the correction as of v2.2. The one twin that was expected to differ, G0b, was run as a report-only physics diff and its divergence was attributed to rotation before the fact, not after it.

Benchmark 4 — sphere–wall lubrication crossover (D2.1) RULE v1 DELIVERED

Setup & expectation

A sphere approaching a flat wall feels a drag that diverges as 1/gap — Brenner's 1961 exact solution for perpendicular approach. No fixed mesh can resolve that divergence all the way down, so the practical question is not whether the resolved force falls off the analytic curve but where: below which gap must a sub-grid lubrication correction take over? That threshold is the number every near-contact simulation needs and the one the campaign had been carrying as a guess.

Stage 1 — read it off the ten Cate tails, for free

Every ten Cate run ends with a sphere approaching the bottom wall, so the data already existed. Only E1 is honest here — at Re = 1.5 the approach is quasi-steady (inertia diagnostic 0.04), while E2–E4 are contaminated by unsteadiness rather than resolution. E1 tracks Brenner to within −6…−9% at a gap of one radius, and departs by 20% at a gap of 1.2–1.3 h. Provisional, and already 4× less conservative than the ad-hoc threshold in use. RECORDED

Stage 2 — the definitive constant-velocity protocol

The free variant confounds approach speed with gap. Driving the sphere at constant V = 0.02 (μ = 0.373, Re = 0.78, via the heavy-sphere trick below) removes the inertia confound entirely, and the agreement over the mid-range tightens to ±2–5% for gaps of 0.25 R to 2 R. The departure points then land cleanly, and refinement moves them the right way — at a fixed absolute gap the error shrinks with h (at ε = 0.1: L3 −19.2%, L4 −12.7%). RECORDED

Where the resolved force leaves the lubrication asymptote
Departure L3 (D/h 23.9) L4 (D/h 49.1)
−10%gap = 2.1 hgap = 2.8 h
−20%gap = 1.1 hgap = 1.7 h
Crossover rule v1

The resolved FBM force stays within ~10% of the lubrication asymptote down to a gap of about 2–3 cells, and degrades rapidly below ~1.5 cells. So a sub-grid correction should take over at gap ≲ 2 h — expressed in cells, not in absolute length, which is what makes it portable across meshes.

This supersedes the ad-hoc 5·h_min threshold the code carried, which is 2.5× more conservative than the measurement warrants — it was handing over to a model while the mesh was still resolving the physics correctly. Note that HCAF has no lubrication of its own (the API stubs no-op), so this rule is the measured input to the D2.2 shared-closure component rather than a tuning of something already running.

D1.2 — the grid-crossing noise floor is first order in h

Setup & expectation

As a particle translates, the 0/1 indicator re-classifies mesh points and the FBM force integral jitters. That jitter is the method's intrinsic noise floor, and until it is measured every moving-particle tolerance on this page is a guess. Measuring it needs motion without dynamics: a sphere driven at constant velocity so any wobble in the force is the mesh talking, not the physics.

It halves with every refinement

A controlled ladder at fixed V = 0.1 in the E4 fluid gives rms detrended force noise of 3.84% / 1.79% / 0.88% of the mean at D/h = 11.4 / 23.9 / 49.1 — successive ratios 0.47 and 0.49. The noise floor is first order in h, cleanly. The free-fall plateaus of the existing ten Cate runs give 4.1 / 2.4 / 0.9% independently, which agrees. RECORDED

  • practiceExpect ~1%-class force jitter at the D/h ≈ 24 workhorse resolution, and ~4% at smoke grade. That is the honest floor for every moving-particle gate in the campaign — tolerances tighter than it are measuring noise.
  • PASSThe enabler: a prescribed-motion protocol — heavy sphere (ρ_p/ρ_f = 10⁶) with gravity off, initialParticleVelocity_ (an EL-era key that was parsed but never applied in the bench setup) and benchUseConfigStart_. Velocity holds constant to 0.0013% over the run, and the keys are twin-certified as a strict no-op when absent.

Benchmark 5 — dt-floor probes

Setup & expectation

The ten Cate configuration re-run at the density ratios the DKT case uses (ρ_p/ρ_f = 1.10 and 1.02, i.e. particles barely heavier than the fluid), with the sawtooth watchdog armed. Near-neutral buoyancy is the hardest regime for an explicitly coupled fluid–solid scheme, so these are cheap stability checks run before committing to the expensive pair simulations. The expectation is simply a clean, warning-free trajectory at the timesteps the production runs will use.

  • PASSBoth ratios are clean at dt = 1 ms: 0 warnings, plateau jitter 5 × 10⁻⁶…4 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, and sensible settling (ratio 1.10 → −0.082, ratio 1.02 → −0.018 at t = 0.6).
  • PASSRatio 1.10 at dt = 0.5 ms agrees with the dt = 1 ms trajectory to 0.3–0.5% through the whole transient, with 0 warnings — no floor above 0.5 ms at this ratio.

Benchmark 6 — the numerical viscometer, V2 through-hole cell (D5.1 rheology arc) BASELINE + φ LADDER 4 / 4 PASS LUBRICATION PAIRS RESOLVED

Setup & expectation

This is a rebuilt instrument. An earlier blind-bore cell — closed at both ends, with the bob immersed only part-way — was retired on 2026-08-26 because 45.7% of its baseline torque was generated in fluid the particles never reach, which dilutes η(φ) = T(φ)/T(0) by an unmeasurable factor and leaves the Einstein gate unable to discriminate. The full trail is in the datasheet rows d51_*; nothing measured on that cell is carried forward here.

The replacement runs the hole through the entire height and makes both end planes symmetry planes. The flow is then an axially uniform annular Couette — quasi-2D, no rings, no end faces — and the only particle-free zones left in the cell are the modelled packing margins. Two things follow, and both are gates: the geometry earns an exact analytic torque reference the blind bore never had, so the empty baseline can be checked against a number rather than only against itself; and η(φ) is undiluted, so the φ = 0.05 gate finally discriminates.

The rung is still the Einstein gate — a dilute suspension must return the viscosity a mean-field theory says it should — and the cell is still the entry point to the D6 Kroupa-box capstone, which is a μ_eff(φ) case end to end. V2.0 is the φ = 0 baseline, the denominator every later ratio divides by; V2.1 is the gate itself, 225 spheres at φ = 0.05.

V2.0 reading — the corrected reaction estimator lands on the analytic value PASS

Gate 3 did more than pass. RES + 31.416 = 83.774 against T_exact = 83.78 is a deviation of −0.008% — the corrected reaction estimator reproduces the analytic torque to five digits. That pins the +0.54% carried by the deformation-form estimator as volume-quadrature discretization error in DNA, not a physical excess: two estimators with different error structures, and the analytic reference tells you which one is drifting. This is the separation a two-estimator protocol exists for, and the blind bore could never have produced it because it had no exact reference to check against.

The baseline is certified. T(0) = −84.2296 is the denominator every η below divides by.

Why gate 1 is new, and why gate 3 needs a correction constant

Gate 1 exists only because the geometry is axially uniform. A blind bore has end faces and a lid, so its torque has no closed form and the baseline can only be checked for reproducibility; a through-hole annulus with symmetry ends has an exact solution, so discretization error is the only thing left to excuse a mismatch — hence the tight 3%.

Gate 3 carries the campaign's physical-torque protocol. FF assembles the Newtonian viscous operator in gradient (Laplacian) form, so the reaction estimator measures the gradient-form boundary flux and misses the transpose term. For translation that difference integrates to zero over a closed surface; for a rotating Dirichlet surface it does not — rigid rotation has curl 2Ω, and the missing term is exactly 2μΩV_enclosed. Here V_hole = πrᵢ²H = 785.4, so the constant is 31.416.

Rebuilt as a through-hole annulus, the same solver at the same production resolution validates Einstein viscosity quantitatively at φ = 0.05. Two deviations from ladder standard are on the record rather than smoothed over: at φ = 0.20 the RSA packing was relaxed to 1.01 d minimum pair distance and 0.25 d clearances because 900 spheres reach the RSA saturation limit at the ladder's 1.05 d / 0.5 d setting; and that rung ran on the twin-certified build-twin-pe6e5ba9c binary (pe 9d24437) rather than the frozen f9b7115, with the bitwise-equivalence chain (jobs 141389 / 141658) keeping the T(0) ratio valid. Local concentration reaches φ = 0.315 at φ = 0.10 and 0.415 at φ = 0.20, so the composites are evaluated pointwise rather than at the global φ.

The ladder finding — each rung lands on the closure valid at its own concentration PASS

Three rungs, three different closures, no tuned parameters anywhere: +0.60% against Einstein at φ = 0.05, −0.78% against Batchelor at 0.10, −0.94% against Krieger–Dougherty at 0.20. Just as telling is where each rung fails to match: at φ = 0.10 the measurement sits +4.4% above the Einstein composite, and at 0.20 +5.6% above the Batchelor composite. First-order theory does not merely become imprecise — the instrument resolves the O(φ²) hydrodynamic interaction term as a physical effect, and then resolves the point where the truncated series itself runs out.

That is the campaign claim the rheology arc was built to support: at production resolution, D/h ≈ 8, this DNS reproduces suspension viscosity across a 4× concentration range spanning three closure regimes, each inside its own validity window. It is also the honest boundary — the agreement at φ = 0.20 is with a concentrated closure, so nothing here licenses extrapolating a dilute law past its range.

Metrology — the transpose constant, eight times over PASS

The DNA − RES estimator gap has now been measured at every rung of the ladder and with sub-grid lubrication both on and off: −31.4152, −31.4153, −31.4157, −31.4157, −31.4153, −31.4153, −31.4157 — against a predicted −31.416, to five digits, eight consecutive times, with 225, 450 and 900 spheres in the gap and across both lubrication extensions. The transpose term 2μΩV_enclosed therefore depends only on the enclosed, particle-free hole volume: neither the suspension filling the gap nor the lubrication model touches it. A parameter-free prediction, confirmed under loads it was never fitted to — which is what licenses the corrected reaction estimator to ride along as an independent check at every rung.

Sub-grid lubrication pairs — first production use of the D2.2 add-on RESOLVED — both rungs settled

Design — controlled single-variable twins

Each pair is the same run twice: identical particle cloud, identical deck, identical binary, identical restart. The only difference is the json lubrication keys — lubricationEnabled_ true with the kroupaDeficit model and mesh clamp c = 2, giving an activation gap of 2h = 0.2186 in d = 1 units with PE_LUB_MESHDX armed. Nothing else moves, so the difference in η is the sub-grid lubrication contribution and nothing else. The model itself was certified separately in D2.2 (rows d22_g2b_deficit, d22_g3_tencate); this is its first use at suspension scale.

Resolved — the lubrication delta does decay, and it tracks the pair count RESOLVED

What was suspected. On the first segments the two deltas came back statistically indistinguishable — +2.49% at φ = 0.10 against +2.58% at 0.20 — despite four times fewer near-contact pairs, which would have meant the delta was set by a few closest films rather than by how many pairs there are. That reading was held open on the record, because the φ = 0.10 run had the worst plateau anywhere on the ladder.

What the extensions showed. The caveat was right. Extended to t = 300, the φ = 0.10 delta collapses from +2.49% to +0.76%: the segment-1 trace had spiked to η ≈ 1.29 around t ≈ 255 and then stepped down to a flat band — the signature of lubrication-slowed microstructure relaxation, sampled before it finished. The φ = 0.20 delta moved the other way and only slightly, +2.58% → +2.71%, confirming the recorded lower-bound reading of its unplateaued first segment.

The headline. Sub-grid lubrication adds +2.7% at φ = 0.20 and +0.8% at φ = 0.10 at D/h ≈ 9. That is a 3.6× decay against a 3.5× drop in active near-contact pairs (1065 → 302). Naive pair-count scaling was right; the closest-films hypothesis is retired.

One structural detail worth keeping: at φ = 0.20 the saturated fraction grew from 20% to 33% between the first segment and the extension — films tightening under sustained shear as the microstructure ages. The delta is stable across that change, which is part of why the ± 0.3 pp bounce reads as fluctuation rather than drift.

D0.6 DNS constraint-solver decision architecture gate, agreed 2026-07-31

  • DNS and EL do not share a CollisionSystem. HardContactEulerLagrange is EL-specific at its core (hydro forces enter as dv_/dw_ velocity corrections inside the PGS sweep; the FBM path instead injects resolved forces via setForcesMapped through the standard force→integration pathway). DNS gets its own solver — a dedicated HardContactDNS, starting from HardContactSemiImplicitTimesteppingSolvers, HardContactLubricated or HardContactAndFluid; the choice is recorded as a short design note in the report.
    Empirical confirmation (2026-07-31, campaign day one): a fresh build tree inheriting pe master's default (HardContactEulerLagrange) produced an all-zero sedimentation trajectory — force and velocity exactly 0 for 10 steps, no error raised — because setForcesMapped forces are a dead end in that solver. Interim campaign selection until HardContactDNS exists: HardContactAndFluid via cmake -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-Dpe_CONSTRAINT_SOLVER=pe::response::HardContactAndFluid" (the define is #ifndef-guarded; no submodule edit needed). The zero-trajectory signature is now a documented failure mode.
  • Share components, not the class: (a) the Kroupa lubrication closure functions become a solver-agnostic pure-math component both solvers call (with different policy — see D2.2); (b) the accumulator/audit machinery (contact virial, per-wall impulses, Newton-pair bookkeeping) becomes free-standing, exposed through the pe/interface/el_optional_api.h detector pattern so the Fortran query chain works against whichever solver implements it. The detector refactor at the end of the EL branch is exactly what makes this cheap.
  • Equivalence twin before any campaign numbers: E4 sedimentation (10-step smoke + full trajectory) under HardContactEulerLagrange vs the DNS solver, same inputs. Bitwise identity is not expected across solvers — the gate is trajectory agreement within the D1 noise floor, with the wall-contact phase compared and RECORDED.
  • Operational consequence: one build = one pe_CONSTRAINT_SOLVER, so DNS and EL campaign binaries come from separate build trees; every D5 cross-comparison row records which binary/build produced each side.

D1.1 Fixed-sphere resolution ladder no moving boundary — cleanest signal CLOSED

The measured asymptotic order came out near first — as expected for a staircase indicator method, and now measured rather than assumed. The same error model then checks out at a second volume fraction (φ = 0.0082, −1.52%, was −19.2%), which closes the last open thread on this case. Getting there required D1.1b below.

  • Case: periodic simple-cubic sphere array at low φ, Stokes/low-Re flow, q2p1_dns_drag machinery (serial-PE only today — acceptable; note as constraint). Reference: Hasimoto (1959) dilute-array expansion; Zick & Homsy (1982) / Sangani & Acrivos (1982) tables for general φ.

D1.1b Periodic-coupling anomaly opened by D1.1, fixed 2026-08-03 RESOLVED

Unplanned, and the campaign's most consequential result. D1.1's ladder converging to a wrong asymptote was treated as evidence rather than noise; the trace found that the Q2 communicator carried no periodic DOF pairs at all, so every periodic face in the code base was solved traction-free. Full narrative, the fix, and its verification gates are in the status section.

  • Fix: a parallel periodic vertex-share table (myVERTLINKPER) built by an all-26-image octree probe and unioned into the Q2 communicator gate — single-axis probing leaves periodic edges and corners partially coupled and diverges.
  • Verified no-op off the periodic path: the walled twin is byte-identical, so no walled result in the campaign moves.
  • Enforced going forward: periodic decks require axis-uniform Cartesian partitions (METIS invalid), and MUMPS is refused as coarse solver on periodic decks.
  • Cross-campaign: this defect affected every “fully periodic” run in both campaigns. The EL momentum-conservation gate has been re-verified on the fixed binary and passes; re-interpretation of the periodicity-dependent EL results is pending.

D1.2 Grid-crossing noise translating sphere, frozen dynamics MEASURED

Measured 2026-08-06. The noise floor is first order in h — rms force jitter 3.84 / 1.79 / 0.88% of the mean at D/h = 11.4 / 23.9 / 49.1, halving per level — with the free-fall plateaus agreeing independently. See the status section. This required the prescribed-motion protocol, which the plan below anticipated as skipFBMDynamics but which landed instead as a heavy-sphere + zero-gravity construction driven from the case json.

  • Observable: force time-series oscillation amplitude vs D/h as the indicator re-classifies DOFs. This characterizes the intrinsic FBM force noise floor — needed to set honest tolerances for every moving-particle gate later (and explains trajectory jitter practitioners see).

D3.1 Static random arrays — DNS drag law highest value/cost ratio CLOSED

Closed 2026-08-11 — the F(φ, Re) surface is measured end to end and every deviation from the reference is accounted for. Random fixed-sphere arrays now load through an opt-in xyzFilePath_ path in the dns_drag setup — twin-certified as a bitwise no-op, so the existing single-sphere and lattice cases are untouched — fed by a seeded RSA generator that applies periodic minimum-image checks. The probe ladder that followed did what probe ladders are for: it found a defect before the production matrix was launched.

Re-opened for audit, then closed again 2026-08-18. Preparing this stage's results for the CHERD journal supplement put them through two internal review rounds and a set of colleague critiques, which surfaced a transient bias in the dilute finite-Re runs and two errata in how the results were transported and described. All of it is documented in the SI hardening audit at the end of this stage. No conclusion changed — but the basis underneath them did, from extrapolated to measured.

The reference — Beetstra, van der Hoef & Kuipers (2007)

The Beetstra paper is not a theory paper; it is a large measurement campaign. The authors ran lattice-Boltzmann flow through static random arrays of spheres over 35 combinations of packing fraction and Reynolds number — φ from 0.10 to 0.65, Re from 10 to 1000, resting on their own earlier Re → 0 dataset — and fitted the result into a drag correlation. That correlation went on to become a standard closure input for Euler–Lagrange and two-fluid models of dense suspensions and fluidised beds, which is to say it is exactly the kind of closure the EL campaign spent two months validating. Measuring the same quantity from the resolved side is the bridge between the two campaigns, and the concrete content of the D5 “DNS-informed EL” deliverable.

The configuration is close to what this machinery already does: N spheres placed at random in a fully periodic cell, non-overlapping and held fixed, with a constant body force — equivalently a mean pressure gradient — driving flow through the array. The measured quantity is the mean drag per particle as a function of φ and Re. Because a random pack is a sample rather than a geometry, the reference is an ensemble statement: no single arrangement is obliged to sit on the curve.

There are conventions to get right, and they are worth stating plainly. Their F is the drag part only. A particle in a driven array feels both surface friction and a buoyancy-like pressure-gradient force −V_p∇P; the correlation excludes the second, so F_d = (1 − φ) · F_total — while a momentum balance, which is what we measure, gives F_total. Their normalising velocity is the superficial U = (1 − φ)u₀ (eq. 1), and their Reynolds number uses that same superficial velocity (eq. 2). The Stokes-limit fit is a modified Carman form, F(φ,0) = 10φ/(1 − φ)² + (1 − φ)²(1 + 1.5√φ) (eq. 6), normalised so that an isolated Stokes sphere gives exactly 1.

As a validation target it plays the part for many spheres that Hasimoto played for one — a genuinely periodic flow judged against something outside our own code. Two things differ. The reference is ensemble-fitted data rather than a closed form, so agreement has to be read against seed scatter as well as against discretization. And the output is not only a check: it is the drag law the EL side needs.

A second periodicity defect — the FBM indicator is not periodic either

This is a sibling of the D1.1b communicator defect, in a different layer, and the probes caught it by a volume audit. A sphere whose centre sits near a periodic face loses the part of itself that lies outside the box: the indicator simply does not wrap. With 8 of 16 spheres straddling a face, the measured solid fraction came out at 0.0441 (L3) → 0.0435 (L4) against a nominal 0.05 — and the giveaway is that it converged the wrong way, toward the Monte-Carlo value for un-imaged geometry, 0.04301. Refinement was faithfully resolving truncated spheres. D1.1 never saw this because its single sphere sits at the cell centre.

Fix for fixed arrays — the generator emits explicit image spheres, which is solver-free and exact. Solid fraction returns to +0.16% (L3) and +0.05% (L4) of nominal, and the flow visibly changes: the superficial velocity drops as it has to squeeze past whole spheres rather than clipped ones. RESOLVED

Recorded limitation. That fix works because the geometry is static. Moving particles crossing periodic faces need real periodic support in the FBM classifier (and in PE), which does not exist yet — flagged for the dynamic D3 stages and for any EL periodic re-run in which particles wrap. RECORDED

Third convention pin — and it accounted for the entire apparent discrepancy

The raw comparison sat +14 to +53% above Beetstra, and the excess grew with φ — which looks exactly like a physics problem, and for a while was treated as one. It was not. Reading the force split off the paper itself (pp. 490–491) fixes F as the drag part alone, so the measured total must be multiplied by (1 − φ) — a correction that grows with φ in precisely the way the discrepancy did. With that applied, and the superficial-velocity normalisation of eq. (1), the excess collapses to single digits at every φ.

This is the third time in this campaign that an apparent result turned out to be a convention — after Hasimoto's F and, separately, his U. The pattern is consistent enough to be a working rule: pin the reference's own definitions, from the reference's own text, before believing a discrepancy. RESOLVED

Agreement within ±9% across the whole surface — except one corner

Eleven of the twelve points sit inside or on the correlation's own ±10% band, most of them well inside, over a six-fold range in φ and from Stokes flow to Re ≈ 27. The exception is sharp and localised: at Re ≈ 27 the three lower packing fractions run −12 to −20% low on this endpoint reading (−12 to −21% once re-measured at steady state — see the SI hardening audit below), while φ = 0.30 stays at +1%. A defect that grew smoothly with Re would look nothing like this. RECORDED

Two candidates, and they are genuinely competing rather than one being the polite version of the other:

  • (a) oursBoundary-layer under-resolution at L4. The viscous layer thins as d/√Re, which at these Reynolds numbers is only 2.5–4.5 cells — and the deficit is largest exactly where D/h is smallest. An under-resolved boundary layer under-predicts drag, which is the sign we see.
  • (b) theirsThe fit's own softness in this range. The paper says so itself: eq. (16) "does not provide a perfect fit", and is "a compromise, where we put the emphasis on the accuracy at higher-Reynolds number, since for low Re the inertial contribution ... is relatively small." Re ≈ 27 is precisely the range they de-emphasised.
  • REPORTEDThe discriminator — an L5 anchor at φ = 0.10 / Re ≈ 30. If the drag rises by roughly 15% on refinement it is (a), our resolution; if it barely moves it is (b), their fit. It came back, and it moved by +1.3%. See below.
The discriminator answers — resolution refuted, and the corner turns out to be microstructure

The L5 anchor ran at the worst point of the whole surface (φ = 0.10, Re ≈ 27, D/h = 33, job 138372, 22 h). Candidate (a) predicted a rise of roughly 15%. The measured shift was +1.3%: seed 1 sits −10.6% at L4 and −9.0% at L5 against eq. (17). The deficit survives at D/h = 33, so boundary-layer under-resolution is refuted — a rare case of a hypothesis being cleanly killed rather than quietly dropped.

What replaced it came from splitting the corner per seed, each read at its own measured Re rather than at a nominal one. The three seeds deviate by −10.6 / −33.2 / −14.0% — a spread far too wide to be numerical. Seed 2's arrangement simply passes much more flow at the same forcing. The reading is that at Re ≈ 27–33 array drag becomes microstructure-dominated: a single 16-sphere configuration can legitimately sit ±10–30% around any ensemble-mean fit, against 3–8% seed scatter in Stokes flow — inertia amplifies configuration sensitivity by roughly 3×. The earlier aggregate “−20%” was an artefact of averaging seeds that were at different Re. RECORDED

Why this matters beyond D3.1 — a closure implication for D5

If instantaneous drag varies by tens of percent with local arrangement once Re ≳ 20, that dispersion is physical, not noise — and it is exactly what a mean-field closure integrates away. Every EL and two-fluid model built on an ensemble-mean correlation carries one number where the resolved flow has a distribution. A DNS-informed EL closure is in a position to carry the fluctuation as well as the mean, which is a capability the correlation literature cannot supply from ensemble fits alone.

The corner, settled — resolution refuted corner-wide RECORDED

The remaining anchors reported (jobs 138501 / 138502, joining 138372). Across the whole corner at Re ≈ 25–29 the L4 → L5 shift is +1.4% / +1.3% / +1.7% at φ = 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.20 — the single-point verdict generalises, and resolution is refuted corner-wide rather than at one lucky spot.

Seed-1 residuals at L5 are −4.2 / −9.0 / −19.1% against eq. (17). What remains is therefore two things, both already named: microstructure sensitivity — the per-seed spread runs −10…−33% at these Reynolds numbers — plus the correlation's own admitted softness in exactly this range. Corner attribution closed.

The Stokes offset — it was finite-size, and the closure is exact enough to be worth stating plainly

At Beetstra's own particle count, N = 54 (jobs 138503 / 138504, φ = 0.10, Stokes, single configuration, L4 D/h = 11 → L5 D/h = 22), the converged FBM value lands at 2.439 against the correlation's 2.428 — +0.4%, where the same quantity at N = 16 sits at +4.1%. The long-standing +4…+11% Stokes offset was the small box talking to its own periodic images: finite-size, not RSA microstructure. That was the last structural candidate standing.

Which licenses the statement this stage was built to earn: two completely different numerical methods — our Q2/P1 FEM fictitious-boundary solver and their lattice-Boltzmann — agree on the random-array drag law at the half-percent level once the configuration ensemble is matched. That is about as strong a cross-method validation as CFD offers, and it is not a coincidence of calibration: both chains trace back to the same Hasimoto 1959 root — their sphere-diameter calibration, our D1.1 closure. PASS

D3.1 exit gate — complete

Every deviation from the reference is now either corrected (resolution, via the a_eff model), quantified (seed scatter, including its ~3× amplification by inertia), or attributed (finite-N at Stokes, microstructure at moderate Re). Nothing is left unexplained — and the production-resolution answer came out of the same runs as a bonus.

The L5 anchors: resolution is not what lifts the Stokes numbers

Four anchors at L5, one per φ, put the Stokes resolution correction at +2.0 to +3.5% — small, and upward. That matters because it rules out the tidy explanation: interface widening cannot be responsible for a positive offset that refinement makes larger. Anchor-corrected, the converged FBM drag law sits +4 to +11% above eq. (6) — which is at or near the correlation's own stated 10% accuracy, so this is agreement at the edge of the reference's resolving power rather than a discrepancy needing a culprit.

The remaining candidates are structural rather than numerical: N = 16 against their N = 54 (finite-size), and an RSA-with-gap microstructure against equilibrium hard spheres — two different ways of being "random". An N-ladder would separate them; it is recorded as the next question, not launched. RECORDED

  • PASSHigh-Re calibration probe — Re = 39.3 with the endpoint perfectly steady (sd/mean 3.4 × 10⁻⁴ over t = 3…4), which is what licenses reading a single endpoint per run instead of time-averaging the whole ladder.
Applied to production resolution — the array-level counterpart RECORDED

The single-sphere probes in Benchmark 2 asked what D/h = 3–4 costs for one sphere. This asks the same question of a crowd, which is the case production work actually runs. The identical p005 and p010 configurations were rerun at L2 — D/h = 3.3 and 4.1 — across all three Re tiers and all three seeds: 18 runs, jobs 138572–138589, minutes each. Because the configuration is held fixed, the comparison is against each config's own L4 value rather than against the correlation, which is the correct production metric.

The expectation going in was that inertia would punish coarse meshes: a boundary layer only a few cells thick at Re ≈ 30 ought to degrade badly. It did not. The deficit is nearly Re-independent — if anything slightly smaller at high Re than in Stokes flow. Mean array drag is dominated by long-range screening between spheres, and a coarse mesh carries that faithfully even when it cannot resolve the individual boundary layers.

SI hardening — the D3.1 audit arc CLOSED 2026-08-18

With D3.1 closed, the campaign turned to hardening the drag benchmarks for the CHERD journal supplement. Two internal review rounds plus colleague critiques put the finite-Re results under pressure they had not seen before, and the audit that followed produced two errata, one discovery, and a 24-run re-measurement campaign. Everything below is that audit. The short version, stated up front because it is the point: every headline number survived, now on a fully measured basis.

The discovery — the dilute finite-Re runs were never steady RESOLVED

The SI needed a steadiness statement for every run, so every run got swept. The dilute ones failed. The relaxation time of a body-force-driven array goes as τ ~ ρ U_ss / (f(1 − φ)), which is large exactly where the forcing is weak and the array is open — so the φ ≤ 0.10 finite-Re runs were still climbing at their t = 4 endpoint. Endpoint-to-steady gaps reach 13.3% (worst: p005_s2_re10): 2.6–13.3% across the φ ≤ 0.10 Re ≈ 9 band, 0.9–8.1% at Re ≈ 27. At φ ≥ 0.20 the runs are fully steady (< 0.2%) — which is why the high-Re calibration probe's clean sd/mean = 3.4 × 10⁻⁴ had licensed endpoint reads in the first place: it was measured at φ = 0.20.

The first response was a gated Aitken / geometric-tail extrapolation pipeline (tools/d31_steady_extrapolation.py): U_ss = U(t_e) + ΔU·r/(1 − r), the construction applied only where the endpoint drift d = |U(t_e) − U(t_e−1)|/U(t_e) exceeds 5 × 10⁻³, at sample spacing s = 1.0. The gate is not decoration — it exists because r → 1 on a near-steady tail amplifies noise without bound, and it later caught exactly that pathology in our own diagnostic.

Superseded by direct measurement — 24 runs to t = 12

An extrapolation is an argument; an asymptote is a measurement. So all 12 dilute finite-Re L4 runs and their 12 L2 twins were rerun to t = 12 (jobs 139696–139717), joined by two L5 Re ≈ 9 refinement checks (jobs 139695 and 139718). The extrapolated surface was then set aside and replaced by the measured one — with the full set retained as a test of the t = 4 construction rather than as the result.

Erratum — the first verification scorecard was partly an artifact of an ungated reference RESOLVED

The initial full-set check reported three Re ≈ 27 exceedances. One of them was ours, not the method's: the t = 12 references had been computed by applying the extrapolation construction ungated at t = 12. On p010_s3_re30, whose t = 12 tail is a post-peak plateau with r = 0.99, that manufactured a spurious −1.1% decline (reference 1.2043 against a true endpoint of 1.2180) — the precise pathology the gate was built to prevent, demonstrated on our own diagnostic.

Recomputed with the certified gated procedure, the corrected scorecard reads: 10 of 12 runs within their assigned per-run uncertainties, with the entire Re ≈ 9 band inside ±0.13%. Two exceedances are real — p005_s2_re30 at +1.13% (3.8× its 0.30% window) and p010_s2_re30 at +0.85% (2.7× its 0.32%) — the two largest-correction Re ≈ 27 seeds, both positive.

Diagnosed, not waved away: the Re ≈ 27 approach to steady state is weakly non-monotone — p005_s2_re30 peaks at t ≈ 10.25 and then settles back by 0.03% — so a monotone geometric model necessarily over-predicts the remaining rise. And the same exceedance appears at L2 (+1.0% / +1.2%): it is correlated across levels, so it cancels to ≤ 0.4 pp in the L2/L4 production ratio the statement is actually built from.

Erratum — matched-Re transport was additive; the consistent form is multiplicative RESOLVED

Comparing L2 against L4 means comparing runs that, at fixed forcing, sat at slightly different Reynolds numbers — so the correlation is used to transport one to the other. The pipeline had done this additively (subtract the correlation's absolute increment), and colleague review forced the operation to be written down explicitly rather than left implicit. Written down, it was the wrong one. The deficit model underlying the whole 1.15–1.20 correction is a factor on drag, and under F_sim ≈ β · F_corr the exact transport is multiplicative:

F*L2,matched = F*L2 · F*corr(φ, ReL4) / F*corr(φ, ReL2)

The assumption it rests on is stated in the SI alongside the formula: the correlation is trusted for the relative Re-dependence over a 10–12% transport interval, not for its absolute level. That distinction is what makes the multiplicative form defensible where the simulation sits 10–20% below the correlation — which is exactly the Re ≈ 27 situation, and exactly where the operation matters, at ~2 pp.

What the audit changed — and what it did not

Three errata and a re-measurement campaign, and the conclusions are where they were: converged fraction 84–87%, production correction factor 1.15–1.20, matched-Re deficits 12–14%. What changed is the basis: extrapolated became measured, assumed became verified, implicit became stated. That is what review pressure is supposed to buy — not different answers, but answers that can be defended line by line. The one number that moved materially, the Re ≈ 27 dilute deviation, moved away from the correlation, and it is reported that way.

Original stage design

  • Case: frozen random sphere arrays in the periodic unit cell (q2p1_dns_drag + a seeding tool for random non-overlapping packs; the current setup enforces 1-diameter gaps — relax to literature-standard minimum gaps, noting the resolution requirement between close spheres from D2).
  • Sweep φ ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4}, Re ∈ {≈0.2, 10, 50}, ≥3 random seeds each (report seed spread as the error bar).
  • Reference: Beetstra, van der Hoef & Kuipers (2007); Tenneti, Garg & Subramaniam (2011); Ergun/Wen–Yu as engineering anchors.
  • Gate: mean drag within the spread of the two DNS correlations (they differ by up to ~15% — the gate is the band, not one curve).
  • This is the primary DNS-informed-EL input (see D5): the same F(φ, Re) table that validates DNS calibrates/replaces Di Felice hindrance in EL.

D3.2 Wall-bounded hindered settling planned scope closed · attribution discriminator answered RECORDED CLOSED

All 12 ladder points are banked, reduced by tools/d32_ladder_analysis.py over the plateau window t = 15–25. The φ ≈ 0.11 tier that was supposed to decide whether a slope fitted over φ ≲ 0.08 was real landed on the line: the collapse holds over the full lever, and the exponent below is a measurement rather than an extrapolation.

Setup & expectation

A random cloud of spheres settles in a walled column — the same geometry family as the DKT case — and the swarm velocity U is divided by the terminal velocity of a single sphere in that same column. That reference is wall-hindered by construction, which is the point: the static confinement then partially cancels in the ratio rather than contaminating it. The expectation is stable hindered settling, U/u_t < 1, against the Rowe/Richardson–Zaki band for an unbounded suspension. The parameters below are pinned across every run in the stage.

Mechanism result — the walls do stabilise it, and that is a cross-campaign statement

The N = 40 smoke gives a clean hindered plateau with the cloud staying coherent, and — the diagnostic that actually matters — an inter-particle velocity spread that saturates rather than growing. There is no runaway clustering. PASS

The same code family produced cluster-induced enhancement, U/u_t > 1, in the EL tri-periodic box (which we now know was solving traction-free faces). Put the particles in a column with walls and the settling is stably hindered. That is direct evidence for the EL campaign's Richardson–Zaki FAIL reframe: hindered settling recovers as soon as the geometry supplies the confinement Richardson–Zaki assumes. Same solver, different box, opposite qualitative behaviour.

1 — The collapse is excellent, and it certifies its own reference

Fitting ln(U/u_t) against ln(1 − φ_cloud) is linear across the entire ladder, with an rms residual of 2.3% — the through-origin fit gives n = 4.57. Freeing the intercept gives n = 4.31 with U/u_t(φ → 0) = 0.978: extrapolated to zero concentration the swarm data recovers the independently measured single-sphere u_t to 2%. That is the internal-consistency check the ladder was designed to carry, and it passes — the measurement chain is sound. Seed spans are only 0.02–0.04 in U/u_t.

2 — But n ≈ 4.3–4.6 sits far above the unbounded-suspension band, and not because of low Re

The Rowe/Richardson–Zaki band for an unbounded suspension is n ≈ 2.7–3.0 at these Reynolds numbers. The measured exponent is far above it. This is not a low-Re effect: the swarm Re stays in the range 51–77 over the whole ladder, squarely where the literature band applies. The near-coincidence with the RZ Stokes-limit exponent 4.65 is explicitly a coincidence — nothing in this data sits in the Stokes limit.

The honest reading is that the walled 6d column measures a confined hindered-settling law, not the mean-field one. The return flow that the narrow walls force through and around the cloud adds hindrance on top of what the unbounded law accounts for. RECORDED

Attribution — the two candidates, and how they were separated RESOLVED 2026-08-22

  • candidateColumn-wall drag on the backflow. Displaced fluid returns through a 6d cross-section, and the walls tax that return path. The single-sphere reference absorbs the static part of this, but not the part that scales with the settling cloud. This one is right — but as collective confinement, not per-particle wall friction.
  • candidateA finite cloud is not a homogeneous suspension. A cloud of bounded extent has to drive its own return flow back through itself; the homogeneous suspension Richardson–Zaki describes does not. REFUTED — the same clouds settle faster than u_t once the walls recede.
  • discriminatorA wider-column ladder — repeat the sweep at larger cross-section. Wall drag scales with the confinement; the finite-cloud term does not, so the two separate cleanly. Built, run and reduced — see the addendum below.
  • discriminatorA genuinely periodic box, which removes the walls outright — but this is blocked today by the known moving-particle periodic-indicator limitation (d31_periodic_indicator): particles crossing a periodic face lose their outside cap, and the fix that works for fixed arrays (explicit image spheres) does not carry to moving ones.
3 — The mechanism gate stays PASS everywhere on the ladder

Inter-particle velocity spread grows with φ — from 11% of U at the dilute end to 27% at N = 120 — but at every single point it saturates in time rather than running away. There is no runaway clustering anywhere on the ladder. That reinforces the cross-campaign story the stage was built to test: the walled column settles stably hindered where the tri-periodic EL box produced cluster-induced enhancement, so confinement is what stabilises hindered settling. PASS

D3.2 closes its planned scope: the mechanism is validated, a tight confined-configuration hindrance law is measured (n ≈ 4.6), and the attribution is settled by the wide-column discriminator below.

Addendum — the wider-column discriminator COMPLETE · RESOLVED 2026-08-22

Design — exactly one variable moves

The sweep is repeated in a 12d × 12d × 24d walled column. Everything else is pinned: same resolution, same certified binary, byte-identical particle clouds copied verbatim from each 6d twin and verified with cmp, and a deck that differs from its 6d twin by exactly one line — the mesh folder. Wall distance is the only thing that changes, which is what makes the two hypotheses separate on a single number. The parameter table above lists both columns; the table below is the answer they gave.

The discriminator logic — what each hypothesis predicts

If the confined exponent n ≈ 4.57 is column-wall drag, quadrupling the cross-section the return flow has to pass through must relax it: the wide column's exponent falls toward the unbounded Rowe band 2.7–3.0.

If it is finite-cloud hindrance — a cloud of bounded extent driving its own return flow back through itself — then the walls were never the mechanism and n stays ≈ 4.5. The two candidates named above separate on a single number, and no other knob was touched that could confound it.

Scope — 7 runs. The two ends of the φ ladder at seeds 1–3, enough for a two-rung exponent, plus a wide-column single-sphere u_t reference: the analysis normalises by the terminal velocity of the same column, exactly as it did at 6d, so the reference has to be re-measured in the new geometry.

Result 1 — an isolated particle is not measurably wall-retarded, so per-particle wall drag is out

The wide-column single-sphere reference (job 140214) matches its 6d counterpart to 0.7%, inside 1σ — the u_t row of the table above — with endpoint drift +2.6 × 10⁻³, well inside the 5 × 10⁻³ steadiness gate. Quadrupling the cross-section does nothing to a single particle at this Re. Whatever the 6d column was taxing, it was not taxing each sphere individually. PASS

Result 2 — the same clouds settle enhanced in the wide column, and the enhancement grows with N

Not weaker hindrance. The opposite sign. The byte-identical clouds that settled hindered in the 6d column come back above U/u_t = 1 in the 12d column, at both rungs and every seed — the two orange markers in the chart above, tabulated seed by seed in the discriminator table. Enhancement growing with particle number is the signature of a collective downdraft — the cloud dragging its own fluid with it — and it is exactly what a finite cloud does when it no longer has to push its return flow past a nearby wall. PASS

Result 3 — the RZ form does not merely shift, it stops applying

Fitting the two rungs in Richardson–Zaki form with the cloud-envelope concentration φ_env — a bounding-box estimate, values in the table above — returns n = −2.63. A negative exponent is not a hindrance law with a smaller number in it; it says the functional form does not describe a finite cloud in a wide vessel at all. RECORDED
